name: Freya Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Freya, 58, and I came into software late with a two-year college diploma. I’m a junior at a tech company making appointment software for small clinics; I still ask a senior to check my changes to reminder messages. I like finding the little barrier that makes a patient give up booking. I use AI every day to explain unfamiliar code and draft test cases, then run the tests myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the job fit life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Omar repairs buses, and our children are grown. My developer pay is on the low side, and his hours vary when the depot is quiet. We have about three weeks of expenses saved and a mortgage, with few similar software jobs nearby. Retirement is in view, but I cannot assume any pension will pay this mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau leaves clinics needing a person to check whether reminders actually reach patients. A neat draft means nothing if the patient never sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about our three-week reserve even if AI barely changes. One quiet spell at the bus depot and an unexpected boiler bill would meet on the same bank statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking reminder changes with a senior and call the clinic desk when a test fails. I’d set aside 40 from each pay packet if the mortgage and groceries are covered. In the first year I’d keep using AI to explain code I do not yet understand, but I would not send patient records into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary bills, not an AI takeover. Our income can wobble while I am still learning the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a receptionist show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A receptionist told me a reminder that arrived at midnight was worse than none. I changed the timing rule after we checked the clinic’s real opening hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending can wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar and I would leave the old sofa alone this year. The first spare money belongs in the bill account, if there is spare money.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking clinic reminders.
I would test **patient delivery** beyond a tidy draft.
think: I worry our **three-week reserve** remains thin even if AI stalls.
I know **depot hours** and mortgage bills can collide.
do: **Keep** checking reminders with a senior and clinic desk.
**Set aside** 40 each payday if essentials are covered.
**Use AI** for code explanations without patient records; defer replacing our sofa this year.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings and variable household hours.
S0.quote: A neat draft means nothing if the patient never sees it.
fieldNote: Her **junior skills** still require senior review, even with daily AI help.
The **three-week buffer** and Omar’s variable depot hours make the mild scenario anxious.

steps.text: Keep testing clinic reminders with a senior and the clinic desk
Save 40 each payday only after mortgage and groceries are covered
Keep the old sofa this year while spare cash goes to bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues Steady Disruption can write and check our routine code before robots alter bus repairs. I would ask the staff union to press for paid learning time and honest figures on junior jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect the company may cut junior hours first, including mine. My daily AI use helps me finish tickets, but it does not give us a month of bills in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the staff union this month and bring examples of clinic reminders that passed an AI check but failed for patients. I’d ask my supervisor for paid time to practise testing appointment flows with the receptionist, and take it only if approved. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d check eligibility for public income help and reduce our takeaway spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours. I can adapt to a new test method, but the mortgage has a fixed date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which patient case would you bring to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A patient with poor eyesight could not find the cancel button on the message. I caught that in a clinic walk-through, not in the generated test list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Omar add hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar can take more depot shifts only when the depot offers them. We would not put his hoped-for overtime into the budget.

I would ask the **staff union** for paid learning time and junior-job figures.
think: I expect my **junior hours** could be cut first.
I know **daily AI use** cannot pay a missed mortgage bill.
do: **Join** the union and show failed patient reminders.
**Practise** clinic-flow testing with receptionist only if paid time is approved.
**Cut** takeaways and check eligible help if my hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours against a fixed mortgage date.
S1.quote: My daily AI use helps me finish tickets, but it does not give us a month of bills in the bank.
fieldNote: She turns **patient failures** into a union case for paid learning and junior-job disclosure.

steps.text: Join staff union and present failed clinic reminder cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 reaches almost all our coding work by 2028, with hands-on repair robots around 2031. Omar’s depot work may last longer, but the booking and parts paperwork will change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my junior post to go. We have less than a month saved, and neither a nearby software vacancy nor retirement income is something I can count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union for the actual layoff timetable and written pay terms, and tell the mortgage lender early if my post ends. I’d stop takeaway meals now and hold any extra cash for the next mortgage payment. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for eligible income support and real local openings that state pay, rather than assume a clinic will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and losing sleep about our mortgage. Two years is not enough to build a retirement cushion from my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your daughter for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown daughter we might need to postpone our visit, not ask her to cover our bills. Her rent is already high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Omar’s work buy time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar would keep repairing buses while paid shifts exist; the robots come later. We would ask the depot about actual shifts, not plan on overtime it has not offered.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach clinic code before 2031 repair robots.
I would tell colleagues **depot paperwork** changes before hands-on repair.
think: I expect my **junior post** to go.
I cannot count on **retirement income** or another local software wage.
do: **Request** union layoff dates and written terms; contact lender if my post ends.
**Stop** takeaway meals and hold cash for mortgage payments.
**Apply** for eligible income help and real paid openings if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless about losing pay with a thin reserve.
S2.quote: Two years is not enough to build a retirement cushion from my current wage.
fieldNote: She expects **coding loss in 2028**; depot repair robots follow around 2031.
She protects the **mortgage** through spending cuts, early lender contact and conditional public help.

steps.text: Stop takeaways; contact lender early if post ends, before a missed mortgage payment
Apply for eligible public income help if dismissed after 2028
Apply to real local paid openings if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 still reaches coding in 2031; hands-on bus repairs face robots around 2034. Five years lets us bargain over paid transitions before junior roles disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think my job could go, but I could test a move into clinic front-desk work while people still need staff. I would not assume the desk survives full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union to negotiate paid job-shadowing with a clinic receptionist and ask the clinic whether it has a real vacancy. I’d shadow only with employer-approved paid time and clinic consent, and apply only if the desk wage plus Omar’s usual hours cover the mortgage. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d take the desk role only if the vacancy and pay still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing code pay, but the extra years give me a way to check a real employer. I would not quit for a promise of a possible desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn at the clinic desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clinic receptionist told me patients sometimes call because a reminder sounds like a threat. I would need to learn that conversation, not just the booking screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which income would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar and I would use his usual shift pay in the calculation. Extra depot shifts and future pension income stay off the page until we can verify them.

I would seek **paid transitions** while junior roles still exist.

I cannot assume **clinic desk work** survives full thinking AI.
do: **Ask** union for paid clinic shadowing and clinic for a real vacancy.
**Shadow** only with employer paid-time approval and clinic consent.
**Apply** after 2031 coding loss only if a real clinic vacancy and combined usual wages cover our mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with time to test a real opening.
S3.quote: I would not quit for a promise of a possible desk job.
fieldNote: She seeks **clinic shadowing** with paid employer time and clinic consent, not an unfunded course.
A **desk move** depends on a real vacancy and income sufficient with Omar’s usual shifts.

steps.text: Ask staff union to negotiate paid clinic shadowing
Shadow receptionist only with approved paid time and clinic consent
Apply after 2031 coding loss only to real clinic vacancy with combined usual pay covering mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 puts our code work at risk in 2036; repair robots follow around 2039. A decade should let us demand actual jobs and funded training, not just course adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I hope to reach a point where retirement is possible, but our current savings are far too thin to assume it. The company could still reduce junior hours well before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stay in the clinic software job while paid hours last, and move 40 from each payday to the bill account if essentials are covered. I’d ask the union each year for junior hours and paid transition places. In the first year after 2036, if my post ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if our verified income and assets actually cover the mortgage and living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the thin cushion even with ten years. Time helps only if the wage keeps arriving and we save some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar and I would review our mortgage balance and any actual retirement income once a year. We would not mark a retirement date on the calendar before seeing those figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should younger colleagues bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger colleagues to keep proof of patient problems they solved. If management cuts training, our union needs cases and numbers, not speeches.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to threaten code before 2039 repair robots.
I would demand **paid training** tied to real jobs over course adverts.
think: I cannot assume **retirement** is affordable from our thin savings and mortgage bills.
I fear **junior hours** could shrink before the full 2036 change arrives.
do: **Stay** in paid clinic work while hours last and save 40 if essentials are covered.
**Ask** the union yearly for junior hours and funded transition places.
**Seek** real paid work if dismissed; retire only if verified resources cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a thin cushion despite ten years.
S4.quote: Time helps only if the wage keeps arriving and we save some of it.
fieldNote: She makes **retirement conditional** on verified income, assets and mortgage costs, with no assumed pension payout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 frightens me most. My junior wage could end before we build one month of savings. Written terms, eligible income help, and paid time to try a real clinic vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the clinic patient has a person to call when the reminder is wrong. A calendar can look full while the waiting room is empty.

headlineQuote: A calendar can look full while the waiting room is empty.
portrait: Freya is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma and three weeks of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily** to learn clinic code but checks patient reminders with senior staff and receptionists.
Her partner’s **bus repair hours** vary, while their mortgage limits what she can risk.
She seeks **union-backed paid shadowing** and a real clinic vacancy before any change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior wage before the household saves a full month.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, eligible income help and paid time to test a real clinic vacancy would help.
